p: Good evening, my dear friend. Euclid is asleep on my lecture notes, so I shall have to do this from memory. Tonight's subject is the cleverest idea in all of arithmetic, and it is so familiar that most people never notice it. It is called place value.
Our road map: first, what place value is. Second, how each place is worth ten times the one beside it. Third, the vital job of zero. And fourth, how to hear large numbers without getting lost.
## Ten digits are enough

We write every number there is with only ten symbols: nought, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight and nine. That is all. Yet with those ten little marks we can write the number of grains of sand on Brighton beach, or the distance to the Moon in inches, should anyone wish to know.

How? Because a digit means different things depending on where it sits. Take the digit 2. In the number 2, it means two. In 20, it means twenty. In 200, two hundred. The digit has not changed. Its place has.

Think of the beads on a shopkeeper's abacus, or the columns in a ledger. The right-hand column is for ones. The next column to the left is for tens. Then hundreds, then thousands. Each column is worth ten times the column to its right.
## Hearing a number in its places
Let us take a number apart. Three hundred and forty-seven.
In plain words: three hundreds, four tens, and seven ones. When we say "three hundred and forty-seven", our language is doing place value for us. "Forty" is four tens wearing a disguise.
?? While I pour, try this. In the number five hundred and sixty-two, how many tens are there?
=> Six tens, which is sixty. The 5 is in the hundreds place, the 6 in the tens place, and the 2 in the ones place.
## Ten times, step by step
Each move one place to the left multiplies by ten. This is why multiplying by ten is so easy: every digit simply moves one place to the left, and a zero fills the empty ones place.

Forty-seven becomes four hundred and seventy. The 4 has moved from the tens to the hundreds; the 7 from the ones to the tens. Mrs Blewitt does this at the greengrocer's without a flicker. I shall use your modern decimal pence. In my day there were twelve pence to the shilling and twenty shillings to the pound, which was splendid exercise for the mind and a torment for children. Ten pounds of potatoes at forty-seven pence a pound? Four hundred and seventy pence, or four pounds seventy, before the grocer has found his slate.
Dividing by ten does the opposite: each digit moves one place to the right.
?? What is three hundred and twenty divided by ten?
=> Thirty-two. Each digit steps one place to the right: the 3 from hundreds to tens, the 2 from tens to ones.
## The heroic zero
Now consider two hundred and five.

There are no tens at all. But we cannot simply leave a gap, for if we wrote 2 and 5 side by side, we should have twenty-five. So we put a zero in the tens place to say: nothing here, but keep the place open. Zero is a placeholder, like a coat left on a seat in a railway carriage.

My Aunt Hester, who kept the most immaculate household accounts in Somerset, distrusted zero. "Much ado about nothing," she called it. But even Aunt Hester had to admit that without it, her accounts would have been in chaos. We shall hear the whole extraordinary history of zero in another lecture.
## Big numbers by ear

Large numbers are grouped in threes, and we name the groups: thousands, millions, billions. A billion, in your century, means a thousand million. In my day the British billion was a million million, and you will still find it so in old books. Your century settled on the smaller one, and I bow to progress.

Say it in groups: two million, five hundred and four thousand, and sixteen. The trick for listening is to catch the group words, million and thousand, as signposts. Everything before "million" counts millions. Everything between "million" and "thousand" counts thousands. And the rest are ones.
?? A harder one, but take your time. If I say "six million and thirty", how many digits does that number have when written?
=> Seven digits: six, then two groups of three. Six, comma, nought nought nought, comma, nought three nought. Plenty of zeros holding places open.
## Why it matters

Before place value, people used systems like Roman numerals, where the symbols add up wherever they sit. Try multiplying MCMXLIV by XXVII in your head. I once tried, during a dull sermon, and gave up somewhere around the second hymn. Place value makes arithmetic into a matter of columns, and columns can be handled one at a time. Almost everything we do in the next few lectures rests on it.
## Summary

Ten digits are enough, because a digit's value depends on its place. Each place is worth ten times the place to its right. Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place left; dividing by ten moves them one place right. And zero keeps empty places open. Next time, we meet the history of that remarkable nothing. Until then, my dear friend, good night.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we go below zero, and I must warn you that my Aunt Hester would not approve. She kept her accounts in a leather ledger, every penny in its place, and she never once wrote a negative number. "Either you have the money, Ambrose, or you do not," she said. "There is no such thing as less than nothing." She was a remarkable woman, but on this point she was wrong.
Our road map: what negative numbers are; the number line; adding and subtracting with negatives; and taking away a negative.
## Less than nothing

Think of a thermometer on a winter morning. Zero degrees Celsius is the freezing point of water. On a cold night the temperature falls below zero: minus one, minus two, minus five. Those are negative numbers. They are perfectly real. The pond is frozen and Euclid refuses to go outside.

Or think of a bank. If you have ten pounds and spend fifteen, the bank, if it is kind, lets you have the money, and your balance becomes minus five pounds. You owe five. Brahmagupta, in India in 628, called negative numbers debts and positive numbers fortunes, and gave rules for both.
## The number line

Picture a long straight road with a milestone marked zero in the middle. To the right, the milestones say one, two, three, and so on forever. To the left, they say minus one, minus two, minus three. This is the number line, and it is one of the most useful pictures in all of mathematics.

The further right, the bigger the number. So minus two is bigger than minus five, because it is further to the right. A temperature of minus two is warmer than minus five. That sometimes feels strange, but think of the thermometer and it becomes obvious.
?? While I pour. Which is colder, minus seven degrees or minus four degrees?
=> Minus seven is colder. It is further down the thermometer, or further left on the number line.
## Adding and subtracting
Adding a positive number means walking right. Subtracting a positive number means walking left. And you may walk straight past zero.
In plain words: start at three, walk five steps left. Two, one, zero, minus one, minus two. You arrive at minus two.
Start at minus four, walk six steps right. Minus three, minus two, minus one, zero, one, two. You arrive at two.

A useful trick: when crossing zero, go to zero first. From minus four, it takes four steps to reach zero, and there are two more steps to take. So you end at two. This is our old friend, bridging through ten, in disguise, bridging through zero.
?? A bank question. You have a balance of minus twelve pounds and you pay in twenty. What is your balance now?
=> Twelve of the twenty pounds clear the debt and bring you to zero. Eight pounds remain. Your balance is eight pounds.
## Taking away a negative
Now for the part that puzzles everyone, including some very distinguished Victorians. What is five take away minus three?

The answer is eight. Taking away a negative is the same as adding. Why? Think of debts. Suppose you are worth five pounds, but that includes a debt of three pounds that you owe. Now someone kindly takes away that debt, cancels it. You are better off: worth eight pounds. Taking away a debt makes you richer.
Or think of the number line. Subtracting means walking left. But subtracting a negative reverses the direction, so you walk right instead.

Notice the brackets around minus three. They keep the minus sign of the negative number attached to it, separate from the minus sign of the subtraction. A little parcel, wrapping up the minus three. Brackets do this job a great deal, and we shall have a whole series of lectures on them before long.
?? Try one. Two take away minus six.
=> Taking away a negative means adding. Two plus six is eight.
## Aunt Hester's objection

Even in my own century, some respectable mathematicians were uneasy with negative numbers. They called them fictitious, or absurd. And yet they appear everywhere: in temperatures, in debts, in heights below sea level, in years before Christ. Aunt Hester never accepted them, but she did keep a separate column in her ledger headed "Owed to the butcher", which, if you think about it, was a column of negative numbers wearing a disguise.
## Summary

Negative numbers are numbers below zero. On the number line, adding moves right and subtracting moves left, and you can walk past zero. Bridge through zero to make it easy. And taking away a negative is the same as adding a positive, just as cancelling a debt makes you richer. Next time we shall tackle the most famous puzzle of all: why minus times minus makes plus. Until then, my dear friend, stay warm, and stay out of debt to the butcher.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight, fractions. I know that word alone has made strong people pale. My retired sea captain in Manchester, a man who had rounded Cape Horn three times, told me that fractions frightened him more than the Southern Ocean. By the end of the term he was doing them for pleasure. So take heart.
Our road map: what a fraction means; the top and the bottom; equivalent fractions; and simplifying.
## Cutting a cake
A fraction is a number that describes part of a whole. Cut a cake into four equal pieces and take one: you have one quarter of the cake.

The bottom number, the denominator, tells you how many equal parts the whole was cut into. Four. The top number, the numerator, tells you how many of those parts you have. One. The words come from Latin: the denominator names the kind of part, quarters, and the numerator numbers them.
Take three pieces and you have three quarters.

The key word is equal. If the cake is cut carelessly into four lumps of different sizes, a piece is not a quarter at all. Mrs Blewitt cuts cakes with a ruler for this very reason, and she has views about anyone who does not.
?? While I pour. A loaf is cut into eight equal slices and you eat three. What fraction have you eaten, and what fraction is left?
=> You have eaten three eighths. Five eighths are left. Three eighths and five eighths make eight eighths, the whole loaf.
## A fraction is also a division

Here is a second way of seeing a fraction. Three quarters also means three divided by four. Share three cakes among four people, and each person gets three quarters of a cake. This is why mathematicians so often write division as a fraction, one number over another.
## Equivalent fractions

Cut a cake in half, and take one half. Now cut each half into two again. You have the same amount of cake, but now it is two quarters. Cut again: four eighths. The amount has not changed; only the name has.

These are equivalent fractions, different names for the same amount. To make one, multiply the top and the bottom by the same number. Multiplying both by two means cutting every piece in two: twice as many pieces, each half the size, so the same amount.
?? What fraction with a bottom of twelve is equivalent to two thirds?
=> Multiply top and bottom by four. Eight twelfths.
## Simplifying
Going the other way is called simplifying. Divide the top and the bottom by the same number. Six eighths: both six and eight can be divided by two, giving three quarters.

To simplify in one step, divide by the highest common factor, which we met in the lecture on factors. Twelve eighteenths: the highest common factor of twelve and eighteen is six. Divide both by six to get two thirds. A fraction that cannot be simplified any further is said to be in its lowest terms.
?? Simplify fifteen twentieths.
=> Both fifteen and twenty divide by five. Three quarters.
## Bigger than a whole

If the top is bigger than the bottom, the fraction is more than one whole. Seven quarters is seven quarter-pieces of cake: four of them make a whole cake, and three more make three quarters of another. So seven quarters is one and three quarters.

Fractions with a top bigger than the bottom are called improper fractions, and numbers like one and three quarters are called mixed numbers. Euclid the cat disapproves of improper fractions on principle. He feels they lack decorum. But mathematicians love them, because they are much easier to calculate with, and when we reach algebra you will see them everywhere.
?? Turn eleven thirds into a mixed number.
=> Three thirds make one whole. Nine thirds make three wholes, leaving two thirds. Three and two thirds.
## Comparing fractions

Which is bigger, three quarters or two thirds? It is hard to say when the pieces are different sizes. So turn them into the same kind of piece. Twelfths will do for both: three quarters is nine twelfths, and two thirds is eight twelfths. Nine twelfths is bigger, so three quarters is bigger, but only just.
## Summary

The denominator says how many equal parts; the numerator says how many we have. A fraction is also a division. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number to get equivalent fractions, and simplify by dividing by the highest common factor. Fractions can be more than one. Next time, we add and subtract fractions, which is all about making the pieces the same size. Until then, my dear friend, cut your cake fairly.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we meet fractions wearing two disguises: decimals and percentages. Underneath the hats, they are the same old friends. Once you see that, a great deal of everyday arithmetic falls into place.
Our road map: decimals as place value continued; converting between fractions and decimals; percentages; and moving between all three.
## Past the decimal point

Remember place value: ones, tens, hundreds, each place ten times the one to its right. Now walk the other way. To the right of the ones place, after a little dot called the decimal point, come tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. Each place is a tenth of the one before.

In plain words: three point four seven means three ones, four tenths and seven hundredths. We read the digits after the point one by one: three point four seven, not three point forty-seven, which helps avoid confusion.

The decimal point was popularised in Europe around 1600; the Scottish mathematician John Napier, whom we shall meet again with logarithms, helped to make it common. Before that, people wrote such numbers in all sorts of awkward ways.
?? While I pour. In the number two point six five, what is the six worth?
=> Six tenths. The first place after the point is tenths.
## Fractions to decimals

Some fractions turn into decimals at a glance. A half is five tenths: zero point five. A quarter is twenty-five hundredths: zero point two five. Three quarters: zero point seven five. A tenth: zero point one.
In general, a fraction is a division, so to turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the top by the bottom. One eighth is one divided by eight, which is zero point one two five.

Some fractions never end. One third is zero point three three three, going on forever. Two thirds is zero point six six six, on forever. These are called recurring decimals. There is nothing wrong with them; they simply refuse to stop talking, like certain members of my college's high table.
## Per cent: out of a hundred
Per cent comes from Latin, per centum, meaning out of each hundred. Twenty-five percent means twenty-five out of a hundred, or twenty-five hundredths.
In plain words: twenty-five percent, twenty-five hundredths, one quarter, and zero point two five are all the same amount, in different hats.

To turn a decimal into a percentage, multiply by a hundred: zero point four becomes forty percent. To turn a percentage into a decimal, divide by a hundred: seven percent becomes zero point zero seven.
?? What is zero point three as a percentage, and as a fraction?
=> Thirty percent, which is three tenths.
## The ones worth knowing by heart

A handful of equivalents come up again and again, and are worth keeping in your waistcoat pocket. One half: zero point five, fifty percent. One quarter: zero point two five, twenty-five percent. Three quarters: zero point seven five, seventy-five percent. One tenth: zero point one, ten percent. One fifth: zero point two, twenty percent. One third: about zero point three three, about thirty-three percent.
## Finding a percentage of something

Ten percent is one tenth, so ten percent of anything is found by dividing by ten. Ten percent of forty pounds is four pounds. From there you can build almost anything. Five percent is half of ten percent: two pounds. Twenty percent is double ten percent: eight pounds. Fifteen percent is ten percent plus five percent: six pounds.
?? Find thirty percent of sixty pounds.
=> Ten percent of sixty is six. Thirty percent is three times that: eighteen pounds.
## Ratio, in brief

Finally, a word on ratio, which compares one amount with another. If a recipe uses two cups of flour for every one cup of sugar, the ratio of flour to sugar is two to one. Ratios are fractions in yet another hat: the flour is two thirds of the mixture and the sugar one third. We shall give ratio a lecture of its own soon.
## Summary

Decimals continue place value past the point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. A fraction becomes a decimal by dividing top by bottom. Per cent means out of a hundred. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three hats on the same head. And ten percent is a tenth, from which everything else can be built. Next time, percentages in daily life: discounts, increases, and the dreaded interest. Until then, my dear friend, keep your waistcoat pocket well stocked.

Good evening, my dear friend. Euclid has knocked my inkwell over, which is a sign that he wants us to work without paper tonight. Very well: tonight we add and subtract bigger numbers entirely in the head.
Our road map: adding by places; carrying; subtracting by places, and the business of exchanging; and a few rules about order.
## Adding by places
Place value, our old friend, is the key. To add two hundred and forty-six to one hundred and thirty-eight, split each number into its places, and add like with like.
Hundreds first: two hundred and one hundred make three hundred. Then tens: forty and thirty make seventy. Then ones: six and eight make fourteen. Now gather them up.

In plain words: three hundred, seventy and fourteen make three hundred and eighty-four. Notice that I added the big parts first. On paper, schoolmasters teach you to start from the ones on the right. In the head, it is usually easier to start from the left, because then you hear the size of the answer straight away.
?? While I pour the tea: three hundred and twenty-five plus two hundred and forty-one.
=> Hundreds: five hundred. Tens: twenty and forty make sixty. Ones: five and one make six. Five hundred and sixty-six.
## Carrying

When a column adds to ten or more, the extra ten belongs to the next place. In our first example the ones made fourteen, which is one ten and four ones. So the one ten joined the seventy, making eighty, and the four stayed in the ones.

On paper, this is called carrying. A little 1 is written above the next column, like a passenger hopping onto the next carriage. In the head, you do it by simply adding the parts at the end, as we did.
?? Try one with carrying. Fifty-seven plus thirty-six.
=> Tens: fifty and thirty make eighty. Ones: seven and six make thirteen. Eighty and thirteen is ninety-three.
## Subtracting by places
Subtraction by places works nicely when each digit on top is bigger.
Five hundred take two hundred is three hundred. Eighty take forty is forty. Seven take three is four. Three hundred and forty-four.

But what about sixty-two take away twenty-seven? The ones are awkward: two take away seven will not go, not in whole numbers. On paper, you exchange. You break one of the six tens into ten ones, so the number becomes fifty and twelve. Then twelve take seven is five, and fifty take twenty is thirty. Thirty-five. Schoolmasters once called this borrowing, though nothing is ever paid back, and Mrs Blewitt disapproves of borrowing on principle.
In the head, there are friendlier ways. You might take away thirty, which is easy, and then give back the three you took too many.
In plain words: sixty-two take thirty is thirty-two; but we only meant to take twenty-seven, three fewer, so add three back. Thirty-five.
Or count up, as shopkeepers do. From twenty-seven up to thirty is three. From thirty up to sixty-two is thirty-two. Three and thirty-two is thirty-five.
?? Your turn, any method you like. Ninety-one take away forty-six.

=> One way: ninety-one take fifty is forty-one, then add back four, since we took four too many: forty-five. Counting up: forty-six to fifty is four, fifty to ninety-one is forty-one, four and forty-one is forty-five.
## Rules of order

Adding has a lovely property: the order does not matter. Three and five is the same as five and three. Mathematicians call this the commutative law, from a Latin word meaning to exchange. You can use it freely: if you must add two and ninety-eight, start with the ninety-eight and add two.

Also, when adding several numbers, you can group them however you please. This is called the associative law. So seventeen and twenty-six and three? Put the seventeen and three together first to make twenty, then add twenty-six. Forty-six.

Subtraction has neither property. Ten take three is seven, but three take ten is not seven. It is minus seven, a number Aunt Hester refused to admit existed. We shall meet such numbers properly in a later lecture, and be kinder to them than she was.
?? Use grouping. Twenty-eight plus fifteen plus twelve.
=> Put twenty-eight and twelve together to make forty. Then add fifteen. Fifty-five.
## Summary

Add by places, big parts first, and gather up at the end. When a column makes ten or more, the extra ten moves to the next place. Subtract by places, or take away a round number and give back the difference, or count up. And remember: addition does not care about order, but subtraction cares very much. Next time, the times tables, and the hidden patterns that make them easy. Until then, my dear friend, good evening.

Good evening, my dear friend. Mrs Blewitt has just returned from the market with twenty-three eggs, having been told they were two dozen, and she is not pleased. Tonight we multiply bigger numbers, which will help her compose her letter of complaint.
Our road map: splitting a number into its places; multiplying by tens and hundreds; the grid method for two-digit numbers; and rounding and adjusting.
## Splitting into places
Suppose we want twenty-three times four. Split twenty-three into twenty and three. Four lots of twenty is eighty. Four lots of three is twelve. Add them.

In plain words: multiply each part separately, then add the pieces together. This works because multiplying spreads out over adding, which mathematicians call the distributive law. We shall meet that law again, with brackets, in the foothills of algebra, and it will be a great friend.
?? While the kettle boils. Thirty-two times three.
=> Thirty times three is ninety. Two times three is six. Ninety-six.
## Multiplying by tens

To multiply thirty by forty, multiply three by four to get twelve, and then deal with the tens. Thirty is three tens and forty is four tens, so we have twelve lots of ten tens, which is twelve hundreds.

The quick rule: multiply the front digits, then put on as many zeros as there were altogether. Three times four is twelve; one zero in thirty and one in forty, two zeros in all: one thousand two hundred.
?? Try sixty times seventy.
=> Six times seven is forty-two, and two zeros make four thousand two hundred.
## The grid in your head

Now a bigger one. Twenty-four times thirteen. Picture a rectangle, twenty-four long and thirteen wide, and imagine dividing it into four smaller rectangles. Split twenty-four into twenty and four, and thirteen into ten and three.
Twenty times ten is two hundred. Four times ten is forty. Twenty times three is sixty. Four times three is twelve. Add the four pieces.

In plain words: every part of the first number meets every part of the second, and we add up all the meetings. That is the grid method. It is exactly what long multiplication on paper does, only spoken aloud and arranged in a friendlier way. Later, when we expand brackets in algebra, you will find it is precisely the same idea, with letters in place of numbers.
?? Your turn. Fifteen times twelve. Split fifteen into ten and five, and twelve into ten and two.
=> Ten times ten is a hundred. Five times ten is fifty. Ten times two is twenty. Five times two is ten. Altogether a hundred and eighty.
## Rounding and adjusting

Sometimes a number is just shy of a round one, and we can be crafty. Nineteen times six? Nineteen is twenty minus one. Twenty sixes is a hundred and twenty. But we have counted one six too many, so take it off.

Shopkeepers love prices like ninety-nine pence for exactly this reason: it sounds less than a pound. But you, my friend, will not be fooled. Four items at ninety-nine pence? Four pounds, less four pence: three pounds ninety-six.
?? Four items at ninety-eight pence each. What is the total?
=> Four pounds, less four lots of two pence, which is eight pence. Three pounds ninety-two.
## A note about doubling and halving

Here is a trick Mrs Blewitt swears by. If one number is even, you may halve it and double the other, and the answer is unchanged. Sixteen times five? Halve the sixteen to eight, double the five to ten. Eight times ten is eighty. You can keep going: forty-eight times twenty-five is twenty-four times fifty, which is twelve times a hundred, which is twelve hundred.
## About Mrs Blewitt's eggs

Back to our complaint. Two dozen eggs should be two times twelve, which is twenty-four. She received twenty-three. One egg short. At, let us say, twenty-five pence an egg, she is owed twenty-five pence, and I pity the poultryman.
## Summary

Split numbers into places and multiply each part, then add. Multiply by tens by multiplying the front digits and adding zeros. For two-digit numbers, picture the grid: every part meets every part. And use rounding and adjusting, or halving and doubling, to make things easier. Next time: division, sharing, and the mysteries of the remainder. Until then, my dear friend, count your eggs.
Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we share things out fairly, which is a subject dear to the heart of anyone who has ever had brothers and a single cake. Division.
Our road map: two ways of thinking about division; how it undoes multiplication; dividing bigger numbers in parts; and what to do with the leftovers, the remainders.
## Two ways to think about it

Twelve divided by three can mean two things. It can mean sharing: twelve biscuits shared fairly among three people, so each gets four. Or it can mean grouping: how many groups of three can you make from twelve? Four groups. The answer is the same, four, but the pictures are different, and sometimes one picture is more helpful than the other.

That sign, a little line with a dot above and below, is called the obelus. It was first used for division in print in 1659, by a Swiss mathematician named Johann Rahn. In much of mathematics we write division as a fraction instead, twelve over three, and you will hear that more and more as we climb.
## Undoing multiplication
Division undoes multiplication. If six sevens are forty-two, then forty-two divided by seven is six, and forty-two divided by six is seven. Three numbers, bound together in a little family.
So every times table you know is also a division table, for free. When someone asks what fifty-six divided by eight is, ask yourself instead: eight times what makes fifty-six? Seven.
?? While I pour. Seventy-two divided by nine.
=> Nine times eight is seventy-two, so the answer is eight.
## Dividing in parts
For bigger numbers, split them into parts that divide easily. Eighty-four divided by four? Split eighty-four into eighty and four.
In plain words: eighty shared among four is twenty each, and four shared among four is one each, so each share is twenty-one.

The trick is to choose the split cleverly. Ninety-six divided by four? Ninety does not divide nicely by four, but eighty does. So split ninety-six into eighty and sixteen. Eighty divided by four is twenty, sixteen divided by four is four. Twenty-four.
?? Try a hundred and twenty-six divided by six. Choose a split you like.
=> Split into a hundred and twenty and six. A hundred and twenty divided by six is twenty, and six divided by six is one. Twenty-one.
## Halving and halving again
To divide by four, halve twice. To divide by eight, halve three times. A hundred and twelve divided by eight? Half is fifty-six, half again is twenty-eight, half again is fourteen.
Dividing by five is doubling and then dividing by ten. Eighty-five divided by five? Double eighty-five is a hundred and seventy, divided by ten is seventeen.
## Remainders
Sometimes things do not share out exactly. Fourteen biscuits among four people: each gets three, which uses twelve, and two are left over. Those two are the remainder.
⟦14\div 4=3\text{ remainder }2⟧

What to do with the remainder depends entirely on the situation, and this is where common sense must accompany arithmetic. If the leftovers are biscuits, you might break them in halves: each person gets three and a half. If they are people waiting for a carriage that holds four, and fourteen people are waiting, you need four carriages, not three and a half, or two passengers walk. If they are eggs being packed in boxes of six, you fill two boxes and have two eggs over.
?? A railway question. Thirty people must travel in compartments that seat eight. How many compartments are needed?
=> Thirty divided by eight is three, remainder six. Three full compartments take twenty-four people, and six more need a fourth. So four compartments.
## Dividing by zero

One word of warning, which we met with Brahmagupta. You can never divide by zero. Why? Because division undoes multiplication. Six divided by zero would have to be some number which, multiplied by zero, gives six. But anything times zero is zero. There is no such number. Dividing by zero is not merely difficult; it is meaningless. Your century's calculating machines, I am told, display an error, or a grumpy word, when you try.
## Summary

Division is fair sharing, or counting groups. It undoes multiplication, so every times table is a division table too. Divide bigger numbers by splitting them cleverly, or by halving repeatedly. Remainders must be handled with common sense. And never, ever, divide by zero. Next time, we shall go below zero, into the land of negative numbers, which my Aunt Hester refused to visit. Until then, my dear friend, share fairly.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we take numbers apart to see what they are made of, rather as a watchmaker opens a watch. Euclid the cat once opened my watch, but he could not put it back together, which is the difference between a cat and a mathematician.
Our road map: factors and multiples; prime numbers as building blocks; breaking a number into primes; and the highest common factor and lowest common multiple.
## Factors and multiples

A factor of a number is a number that divides into it exactly, with nothing left over. The factors of twelve are one, two, three, four, six and twelve. You can arrange twelve chairs in one row of twelve, two rows of six, three rows of four, and so on. Each arrangement shows a pair of factors.
A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. Multiples of four are four, eight, twelve, sixteen, and on forever.
So the two words are opposite sides of one coin. Four is a factor of twelve. Twelve is a multiple of four.
?? While I pour. What are the factors of eighteen? Think in pairs.
=> One and eighteen, two and nine, three and six. So the factors are one, two, three, six, nine and eighteen.
## Primes, the building blocks

Some numbers have only two factors: one and themselves. Seven, for instance. You can arrange seven chairs only in a single row of seven. Such numbers are called prime. The first few are two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three and twenty-nine.

Notice that two is the only even prime. Every other even number can be divided by two. And notice that one is not counted as a prime. That is a convention, agreed by mathematicians for good reasons, which I shall explain in a moment.

Numbers with more than two factors are called composite, meaning made of parts. And here is the wonderful fact. Every whole number above one is either a prime or can be built by multiplying primes together, and in only one way, apart from the order. Primes are the atoms of arithmetic.
⟦60=2\times 2\times 3\times 5⟧

In plain words: sixty is two times two times three times five, and no other collection of primes multiplies to sixty. This is called the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. That "only one way" is why one is not a prime: if it were, we could throw in as many ones as we liked, and the uniqueness would be spoiled.
## Breaking a number into primes
To find the primes inside a number, keep dividing by small primes. Take eighty-four. Halve it: forty-two. Halve again: twenty-one. Twenty-one is three times seven. So:
⟦84=2\times 2\times 3\times 7⟧
This is sometimes called a factor tree, because you can picture each number splitting into two branches, until every branch ends in a prime leaf.
?? Break thirty into primes.
=> Thirty is two times fifteen, and fifteen is three times five. So thirty is two times three times five.
## Highest common factor

The highest common factor of two numbers is the biggest number that divides both. For twelve and eighteen: the factors of twelve are one, two, three, four, six, twelve; the factors of eighteen are one, two, three, six, nine, eighteen. The biggest they share is six.
This is the number you need to simplify fractions, as we shall see shortly. Twelve eighteenths can be divided top and bottom by six, to give two thirds.
## Lowest common multiple
The lowest common multiple is the smallest number in both times tables. For four and six: four, eight, twelve; six, twelve. The first they share is twelve.

Here is a practical use. Two lighthouses flash, one every four seconds and one every six. They flash together now. When will they next flash together? After twelve seconds, the lowest common multiple. Or two omnibuses leave the same stop, one every ten minutes and one every fifteen. They next leave together after thirty minutes.
?? Two church bells ring, one every three minutes and one every five. They ring together at noon. When do they next ring together?
=> The lowest common multiple of three and five is fifteen. So at a quarter past twelve.
## A word from Euclid, the man not the cat

The Greek mathematician Euclid, who worked in Alexandria about three hundred years before Christ, wrote a book called the Elements, which was used to teach geometry in English schools well into my own century. He also described a beautiful method for finding the highest common factor of two numbers by repeated subtraction, still called Euclid's algorithm, and it is still used inside your century's calculating machines. My cat is named after him, though the cat has done nothing to deserve it.
## Summary

Factors divide exactly; multiples are in the times table. Primes have only two factors, and every whole number above one is built from primes in exactly one way. The highest common factor helps to simplify fractions; the lowest common multiple tells you when things coincide. Next time, a closer look at the primes themselves, and a proof more than two thousand years old that they never run out. Until then, my dear friend, good night.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we add fractions together, and I shall begin with a confession. When I was a boy of nine in Bristol, my schoolmaster asked me what one half plus one half was, and I said, with tremendous confidence, two quarters. I had added the tops and added the bottoms. The schoolmaster did not rap my knuckles, to his eternal credit. He cut an apple in half and asked me to put the halves together. I have never made the mistake since.
Our road map: adding fractions with the same bottom; why we never add the bottoms; finding a common denominator; and subtracting.
## Same bottoms
When the pieces are the same size, adding is easy. Three eighths of a pie plus one eighth of a pie is four eighths of the pie. Count the pieces; the kind of piece stays the same.
In plain words: three slices plus one slice is four slices, and each slice is still an eighth. Four eighths can be simplified to one half.
So the rule is: if the denominators are the same, add the numerators and keep the denominator.
?? While I pour. Two fifths plus two fifths.
=> Four fifths. Two pieces plus two pieces, and the pieces are fifths.
## Why we never add the bottoms

Back to my apple. One half plus one half. If you add the tops and the bottoms, you get two quarters, which is one half. But two halves make a whole apple, not half an apple. Adding the bottoms is like saying that two shillings plus two shillings is four double-shillings. The bottom number is the name of the piece, not a count of anything. You do not add names.
## Different bottoms
Now the real business. One half plus one third. The pieces are different sizes, so we cannot simply count them. We must first cut them into pieces of the same size.

What size of piece will work for both halves and thirds? We need a number that both two and three divide into: a common multiple. Six will do; it is the lowest common multiple. One half is three sixths. One third is two sixths. Now the pieces match.
In plain words: cut the half into three sixths and the third into two sixths; three sixths and two sixths make five sixths.

There is a reliable rule if you cannot see a common denominator at once: multiply the two bottoms together. For thirds and quarters, three times four is twelve. One third is four twelfths; one quarter is three twelfths. Together, seven twelfths.
?? One quarter plus one eighth. Hint: quarters can be cut into eighths.
=> One quarter is two eighths. Two eighths plus one eighth is three eighths.
## Another example, with mixed numbers

Mrs Blewitt is making a pudding and needs one and a half pounds of flour for the pudding and three quarters of a pound for the crust. How much flour altogether? Add the whole numbers first: one pound. Then the fractions: one half plus three quarters. One half is two quarters, so two quarters plus three quarters is five quarters, which is one and a quarter. So altogether, one pound plus one and a quarter pounds: two and a quarter pounds of flour.
## Subtracting
Subtraction works the same way. Make the pieces match, then take away the tops.
In plain words: three quarters is nine twelfths, one third is four twelfths, and nine twelfths take four twelfths leaves five twelfths.
?? Five sixths take away one half.
=> One half is three sixths. Five sixths take three sixths is two sixths, which simplifies to one third.
## A useful habit: estimate first

Before adding fractions, estimate. One half plus one third should be a bit less than one, because a third is less than a half, and two halves make one. Five sixths is a bit less than one. Good. If you had got two fifths, your estimate would have warned you, for two fifths is less than a half, and we started with a half before adding anything. Estimating is the mathematician's umbrella: it does not stop the rain, but it stops you getting soaked.
## Summary

With matching denominators, add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator. Never add the bottoms; they are names, not counts. With different denominators, first change both fractions to equivalent ones with a common denominator, often the lowest common multiple, or simply the two bottoms multiplied. And estimate first. Next time, multiplying and dividing fractions, which, delightfully, is easier than adding them. Until then, my dear friend, good night.

Good evening, my dear friend. I have good news. After the labour of adding fractions, multiplying them is a holiday. You simply multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. There is no need to make the pieces match. I have always found this one of the small injustices of mathematics: the harder-looking operation is the easier one.
Our road map: multiplying a fraction by a whole number; "of" means times; multiplying two fractions; and dividing by a fraction.
## A fraction times a whole number
Three times one quarter is three quarters. Three lots of a quarter-cake. Simple.
⟦3\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}⟧
And a fraction of a number: one quarter of twelve is three. Quarter of twelve biscuits, three biscuits. Notice that "one quarter of twelve" and "one quarter times twelve" are the same thing.
## Of means times
That is a golden rule in arithmetic: "of" means times. Half of a quarter of a cake? Take a quarter of a cake, and cut it in half: you have an eighth.
⟦\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}⟧
In plain words: one times one is one, on top, and two times four is eight, underneath. One eighth. The rule is simply: multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms.
?? While I pour. What is one third of one half?
=> Multiply the tops: one. Multiply the bottoms: six. One sixth. A half cut into three pieces gives sixths.
## Two fractions
Two thirds of three quarters?
Tops: two times three is six. Bottoms: three times four is twelve. Six twelfths, which simplifies to one half.

A useful shortcut: you may cancel before multiplying. There is a three on top and a three underneath, and they cancel each other out, leaving two over four, a half. Cancelling saves big numbers and big headaches.

Notice something curious. Multiplying by a fraction less than one makes things smaller. Two thirds of something is less than the whole of it. This surprises people who learned at school that multiplying always makes things bigger. It does, but only when you multiply by more than one.
?? Three fifths of ten pounds.
=> One fifth of ten pounds is two pounds, so three fifths is six pounds.
## Dividing by a fraction

Now division, which sounds frightening and is not. What is three divided by one half? Ask it as a grouping question: how many halves fit into three? There are two halves in each whole, and three wholes, so six halves.

So dividing by a half is the same as multiplying by two. In general, to divide by a fraction, turn it upside down and multiply. The upside-down fraction is called the reciprocal. The reciprocal of one half is two over one, which is two. The reciprocal of three quarters is four thirds.
⟦\frac{2}{3}\div\frac{3}{4}=\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{4}{3}=\frac{8}{9}⟧
In plain words: dividing by three quarters means multiplying by four thirds. Two thirds times four thirds: tops, eight; bottoms, nine. Eight ninths.
Schoolchildren in your century, I am told, chant "keep, change, flip": keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip the second fraction. A serviceable rhyme, though it lacks poetry.
?? Six divided by one third. How many thirds fit in six?
=> Three thirds in each whole, six wholes, so eighteen. Or six times three, which is eighteen.
## Why flipping works

A quick explanation for the curious. Dividing by four is the same as multiplying by one quarter: sharing among four means each gets a quarter. So dividing by a number is multiplying by its reciprocal. And the reciprocal of a fraction is just that fraction turned over. Nothing more mysterious than that.
## A pudding problem

Mrs Blewitt has six pounds of sugar and her recipe for marmalade uses three quarters of a pound per batch. How many batches can she make? Six divided by three quarters is six times four thirds, which is twenty-four thirds, which is eight. Eight batches. Euclid the cat has expressed no interest in marmalade whatsoever.
## Summary

To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and the bottoms, cancelling first if you can. "Of" means times. Multiplying by a fraction less than one makes things smaller. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Next time, decimals, percentages and ratios, which are fractions in different hats. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we go shopping, and then to the bank. Percentages are everywhere in daily life: in sales, in wages, in taxes, in interest on savings and on debts. A person who understands them is very hard to swindle, and I want you to be very hard to swindle.
Our road map: increasing and decreasing by a percentage; the multiplier trick; a famous trap; and compound interest.
## Discounts and increases
A coat costs eighty pounds, and the shop offers twenty-five percent off. Twenty-five percent is a quarter, and a quarter of eighty is twenty. So the coat costs sixty pounds.

An increase works the same way, but you add. A rent of four hundred pounds rises by five percent. Ten percent of four hundred is forty, so five percent is twenty. The new rent is four hundred and twenty pounds.
?? While I pour. A train fare of thirty pounds rises by ten percent. What is the new fare?
=> Ten percent of thirty is three. The new fare is thirty-three pounds.
## The multiplier trick
Here is a quicker way. Taking twenty-five percent off leaves seventy-five percent. So the sale price is seventy-five percent of the original, which is zero point seven five times it.
And a five percent rise makes the new amount a hundred and five percent of the old, which is one point zero five times it.

In plain words: to increase by five percent, multiply by one point zero five. To decrease by twenty-five percent, multiply by zero point seven five. This one number, called the multiplier, does the whole job in one step, and it will be extremely useful when we come to repeated increases.
?? What is the multiplier for a fifteen percent increase? And for a fifteen percent decrease?
=> For an increase, one point one five. For a decrease, zero point eight five.
## A famous trap
Here is a puzzle that catches nearly everyone. A shopkeeper raises a price of fifty pounds by ten percent, then, feeling generous, reduces it by ten percent. Is it back to fifty?

No. Ten percent of fifty is five, so the price rises to fifty-five. But ten percent of fifty-five is five pounds fifty, so the price falls to forty-nine pounds fifty. The fall was taken from a bigger number, so it was bigger than the rise.
With multipliers: one point one times zero point nine is zero point nine nine. So the price ends at ninety-nine percent of where it started.
Moral: a percentage always depends on what it is a percentage of. Newspapers forget this daily, and politicians, I fear, rely on it.
## Percentage change

Sometimes you know the before and after and want the percentage change. Divide the change by the original amount. A house bought for two hundred thousand pounds sells for two hundred and fifty thousand. The change is fifty thousand. Fifty thousand out of two hundred thousand is a quarter: a twenty-five percent increase.
?? A stock of sixty barrels falls to forty-five. What is the percentage decrease?
=> The fall is fifteen barrels. Fifteen out of sixty is a quarter. A twenty-five percent decrease.
## Compound interest

Now the bank. If you save a hundred pounds at ten percent interest a year, after one year you have a hundred and ten pounds. With simple interest, you would earn ten pounds every year. But with compound interest, the interest itself earns interest. In the second year you earn ten percent of a hundred and ten, which is eleven pounds, giving a hundred and twenty-one. In the third, ten percent of a hundred and twenty-one, which is twelve pounds ten pence, giving a hundred and thirty-three pounds ten.
Each year, we multiply by one point one again.

In plain words: a hundred pounds multiplied by one point one, three times over, gives a hundred and thirty-three point one pounds. The power of three, written as a small raised 3, means "multiplied three times". We shall meet powers properly very soon.

Growth like this starts slowly and then accelerates. At ten percent, money doubles in a little over seven years. A useful rule of thumb, used by bankers for centuries, is the rule of seventy-two: divide seventy-two by the interest rate to estimate the years needed to double. At six percent, about twelve years. At nine percent, about eight.
?? Using the rule of seventy-two, roughly how long does it take money to double at four percent a year?
=> Seventy-two divided by four is eighteen. About eighteen years.

The same mathematics works against you with debts. A debt at a high rate of interest grows just as relentlessly. Mr Dickens, who saw his own father imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea, understood this better than any mathematician. Mr Micawber's famous advice in David Copperfield is pure arithmetic: annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen pounds nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual expenditure twenty pounds nought and six, result misery.
## Summary

To change something by a percentage, find the percentage and add or subtract it, or use a multiplier: one plus the rate for increases, one minus the rate for decreases. A rise and then the same percentage fall does not cancel out. Percentage change is the change divided by the original. And compound interest multiplies by the same multiplier again and again, which makes things grow faster and faster. In a later lecture, on exponential growth, we shall climb much further with this idea. Until then, my dear friend, spend nineteen pounds nineteen and six, and be happy.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we begin something very grand, though it starts small. Powers. You have already met them: when we squared numbers in the times tables, and when Mrs Blewitt's savings grew by compound interest. Tonight we give them a proper introduction, and then meet their shy partners, the roots.
Our road map: what a power is; squares and cubes; roots as undoing; and the startling fact that some roots never end.
## Repeated multiplication
Multiplication is repeated adding. Powers are repeated multiplying. Two to the power of five means five twos multiplied together.
⟦2^{5}=2\times 2\times 2\times 2\times 2=32⟧

The big number at the bottom, two, is called the base. The small raised number, five, is called the power, the index, or the exponent. All three names are in use, which is the sort of thing that makes people distrust mathematicians.

Powers grow astonishingly fast. Two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight, two hundred and fifty-six, five hundred and twelve, one thousand and twenty-four. Ten doublings take you past a thousand. Twenty doublings take you past a million.

There is an old story, which I tell you as a story and not as history, of a king who offered a reward to the inventor of chess. The inventor asked for one grain of rice on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, and so on, doubling each time. The king laughed at so modest a request, until his treasurers worked out that the last square alone needed two to the power of sixty-three grains, more rice than the whole world has ever grown.
?? While I pour. What is two to the power of six?
=> Sixty-four. Two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four.
## Squares and cubes

A number to the power of two is called squared, because that many dots make a square. Five squared is twenty-five: five rows of five. A number to the power of three is called cubed, because that many little blocks make a cube. Three cubed is twenty-seven: a cube three blocks long, three wide and three tall.

Powers of ten are especially friendly, because of place value. Ten squared is a hundred. Ten cubed is a thousand. Ten to the power of six is a million: a one followed by six zeros. The power of ten tells you how many zeros.
?? What is ten to the power of four?
=> Ten thousand. A one followed by four zeros.
## Roots: undoing powers

Every operation in mathematics wants a partner to undo it. Subtraction undoes addition; division undoes multiplication. The square root undoes squaring. The square root of forty-nine asks: what number, squared, gives forty-nine? Seven.

The sign for a square root, which looks rather like a tick with a long roof, is called the radical sign. When I read it aloud I say "the square root of", and if what is under the roof is complicated, I shall say "end root" when the roof ends, with a little low hum at each end if your tones are switched on.
The cube root undoes cubing. The cube root of twenty-seven is three, because three cubed is twenty-seven.
?? What is the square root of a hundred and forty-four?
=> Twelve. Twelve twelves are a hundred and forty-four.
## Roots that never end

Now a shock that shook ancient Greece. What is the square root of two? It is a number which, multiplied by itself, gives two. One squared is one, too small. Two squared is four, too big. So it is between one and two. One point four squared is one point nine six, nearly. One point four one four squared is very nearly two. In fact the square root of two is one point four one four two one three five six, and its digits go on forever without ever settling into a repeating pattern.

The Pythagoreans, followers of Pythagoras in the sixth century before Christ, believed that every number could be written as a fraction, one whole number over another. The discovery that the square root of two cannot be written so is said to have scandalised them. There is a legend that the man who revealed it, Hippasus, was drowned at sea for his trouble. That is a legend, and I would not swear to it in court; but the mathematics is certain. Numbers that cannot be written as fractions are called irrational, which means "not a ratio", not "unreasonable", though they can feel unreasonable at first.
We shall prove that the square root of two is irrational in our lectures on proof, and it is one of the loveliest proofs there is.
## Estimating roots

You can estimate a square root by finding the nearest squares. The square root of fifty? Forty-nine is seven squared and sixty-four is eight squared, and fifty is just above forty-nine, so the square root of fifty is just over seven. About seven point one.
?? Estimate the square root of eighty.
=> Eighty-one is nine squared, so the square root of eighty is just under nine. About eight point nine.
## Summary

A power means repeated multiplication; the base is multiplied by itself as many times as the power says. Squares and cubes are powers of two and three. Powers of ten count zeros. Roots undo powers: the square root of forty-nine is seven. And some roots, like the square root of two, are irrational: their decimals never end or repeat. Next time, we use powers of ten to write enormous and tiny numbers neatly, in standard form. Until then, my dear friend, good night.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we tame the giants and the dwarfs of the number world. The distance to the stars, the number of atoms in a teaspoon, the width of a hair: numbers so large or so small that writing them out in full is a misery of zeros. Scientists use a neat shorthand, called standard form, or in your century's American books, scientific notation.
Our road map: big numbers as powers of ten; standard form; small numbers and negative powers; and calculating in standard form.
## Counting zeros
Last time we saw that powers of ten count zeros: ten to the power of six is a million, a one followed by six zeros. So three million is three times a million.
That is far easier to read and to say. The distance from the Earth to the Sun, about a hundred and fifty million kilometres, becomes one point five times ten to the power of eight kilometres.
## The rule of standard form

A number in standard form is written as a number from one up to, but not including, ten, multiplied by a power of ten. The first part carries the significant digits; the power of ten carries the size.

To convert, imagine sliding the decimal point until there is just one digit before it, and count the places you slide. Four hundred and seven thousand: slide the point five places left, from after the last zero to between the four and the zero. That gives four point zero seven, times ten to the power of five.
?? While I pour. Write sixty thousand in standard form.
=> Six times ten to the power of four. Sixty thousand is six followed by four zeros.
## Small numbers

What about the very small? Here we need negative powers of ten. Ten to the power of minus one means one tenth. Ten to the power of minus two is one hundredth. Ten to the power of minus three, one thousandth.

Why should a negative power mean a fraction? Watch the pattern. Ten to the power of three is a thousand. Ten squared, a hundred. Ten to the power of one, ten. Each step down divides by ten. Carry on: ten to the power of nought is one. Ten to the power of minus one is a tenth. The pattern insists, just as it did with minus times minus.
So five thousandths is five times ten to the power of minus three. The width of a human hair is about a tenth of a millimetre, which is one times ten to the power of minus four metres.
?? Write zero point zero zero zero seven in standard form.
=> Slide the point four places right to get seven. So seven times ten to the power of minus four.
## Calculating in standard form
Multiplying in standard form is a pleasure. Multiply the front numbers, and add the powers of ten.

In plain words: two times four is eight; three zeros and five zeros make eight zeros. Adding the powers works because ten cubed times ten to the five is three tens multiplied, then five more tens multiplied: eight tens in all. We shall make this a law of algebra later on, the first law of indices.

If the front number grows past ten, tidy it. Five times ten cubed, times four times ten squared: five times four is twenty, and the powers make five, giving twenty times ten to the power of five. Twenty is two times ten, so this is two times ten to the power of six.
Dividing works the other way: divide the front numbers, and subtract the powers.
?? Multiply three times ten to the power of four by three times ten to the power of two.
=> Three times three is nine. Four plus two is six. Nine times ten to the power of six, nine million.
## A Victorian enthusiasm

In my day, the astronomers and chemists were finding numbers of a size that alarmed the public. Mr Charles Darwin, in the Origin of Species of 1859, estimated that the weathering of the Weald in southern England had taken some three hundred million years, a figure he later withdrew under criticism, but which shows how vast the numbers of science were becoming. Professor William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, argued over the age of the Earth in hundreds of millions of years. Standard form became the natural language of such quarrels. It is far easier to argue about three times ten to the eight than about three hundred million, at least once the port has gone round.
## Summary

Standard form writes a number as something from one to ten, times a power of ten. Big numbers have positive powers; small numbers have negative powers, because each step down the powers divides by ten. To multiply, multiply the front numbers and add the powers; to divide, divide and subtract. Next, the refresher for those in a hurry, and then a small philosophical breather before the great Brackets primer. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight a lecture with a distinctly culinary flavour, for ratio is the mathematics of recipes. It is also the mathematics of maps, of mixing paint, of sharing an inheritance, and of scaling up a pudding for a college feast. Mrs Blewitt, who once had to make a Christmas pudding for forty, is something of an authority.
Our road map: what a ratio is; simplifying ratios; sharing in a ratio; and direct proportion with the unitary method.
## Comparing amounts

A ratio compares two or more amounts. If a mortar mix uses three buckets of sand for every one bucket of cement, the ratio of sand to cement is three to one. It is written with a colon, and the colon is spoken "to".
The order matters. Sand to cement is three to one; cement to sand is one to three.
Ratios can be simplified like fractions, by dividing all the parts by the same number. Twelve to eight: both divide by four, giving three to two.
?? While I pour. Simplify the ratio fifteen to ten.
=> Both divide by five. Three to two.
## Ratios and fractions

A ratio can be turned into fractions of the whole. If the sand-to-cement ratio is three to one, there are four parts altogether, so sand is three quarters of the mix, and cement one quarter. The trick is to add the parts first, to find the whole.
## Sharing in a ratio
Suppose a legacy of thirty pounds is to be shared between two nephews in the ratio two to three. How much does each receive? Here is the method.

First, add the parts: two and three make five parts. Second, find one part: thirty divided by five is six pounds. Third, multiply: the first nephew gets two parts, twelve pounds; the second gets three parts, eighteen pounds. Check: twelve and eighteen make thirty. Good.
?? Share forty-two biscuits between two children in the ratio three to four.
=> Seven parts in all. One part is six biscuits. The shares are eighteen and twenty-four.
## Direct proportion

Two amounts are in direct proportion if doubling one doubles the other, trebling one trebles the other, and so on. The cost of apples is in direct proportion to the number you buy, at least at an honest greengrocer's.

Here is a splendid method, called the unitary method: find the value of one, then multiply. If five pounds of potatoes cost two pounds fifty, what do eight pounds of potatoes cost? One pound of potatoes costs two pounds fifty divided by five, which is fifty pence. So eight pounds cost eight times fifty pence: four pounds.
In plain words: divide to find the cost of one, then multiply by eight.
?? A recipe for four people uses six eggs. How many eggs are needed for ten people?
=> For one person, six divided by four, which is one and a half eggs. For ten people, fifteen eggs.
## Scaling a recipe

Mrs Blewitt's Christmas pudding recipe served eight, and the college asked for forty. Forty is five times eight, so every ingredient was multiplied by five: a pound of suet became five pounds, and so on. She claims the result was the finest pudding ever served in the hall. The Dean claims he could not move for two days. Both statements may be true.
## Maps and scale

A map is a ratio in disguise. A scale of one to fifty thousand means one centimetre on the map stands for fifty thousand centimetres on the ground, which is five hundred metres. So four centimetres on the map is two kilometres on the ground. The Ordnance Survey, whose maps of Britain were the envy of the world in my day, has been using scales like this since the eighteenth century.
?? On a map with a scale of one to fifty thousand, how far on the ground is ten centimetres on the map?
=> Ten times five hundred metres is five thousand metres, which is five kilometres.
## Inverse proportion, in a sentence

Some amounts go the other way: if three workmen take eight days to build a wall, six workmen take only four days, assuming they do not stand about chatting. Doubling the workers halves the time. That is called inverse proportion. We shall meet it again when we draw graphs in words.
## Summary

A ratio compares amounts, and can be simplified like a fraction. To share in a ratio, add the parts, find one part, and multiply. In direct proportion, doubling one doubles the other, and the unitary method finds the value of one first. Maps and recipes are ratios in disguise. Next time, a word on estimating, and then rounding, so that we always know roughly what an answer should be. Good night, my dear friend, and go easy on the pudding.

Good evening, my dear friend. Last time we praised being roughly right. Tonight we learn to be roughly right in a disciplined way. Rounding is how we tidy numbers so they are easy to say, easy to remember, and honest about how precise they really are.
Our road map: rounding to the nearest ten or hundred; rounding to decimal places; significant figures; and sensible accuracy.
## The nearest ten

To round three hundred and forty-seven to the nearest ten, ask: is it closer to three hundred and forty or three hundred and fifty? Look at the ones digit, seven. Seven is five or more, so we round up: three hundred and fifty.
The rule: look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to. If it is five or more, round up. If it is four or less, round down. Halfway, exactly five, rounds up by convention.
?? While I pour. Round three hundred and forty-seven to the nearest hundred.
=> Look at the tens digit, four. Four or less, so round down. Three hundred.
## Decimal places

To round to one decimal place, keep one digit after the point. Two point seven six, to one decimal place: look at the second digit after the point, six. Six is five or more, so round up: two point eight.

Pi, the famous number from circles, begins three point one four one five nine. To two decimal places it is three point one four, because the next digit is one. To four decimal places it is three point one four one six, because the next digit after one four one five is nine, which rounds the five up to six.
?? Round seven point three nine four to two decimal places.
=> Keep seven point three nine, and look at the next digit, four. Round down. Seven point three nine.

A little care is needed when rounding up makes a nine roll over. Four point nine six to one decimal place: the six rounds the nine up, which makes ten tenths, which becomes a whole one. So the answer is five point nought. We say five point nought, keeping the nought to show we rounded to one decimal place.
## Significant figures

Decimal places are not always the right tool. The distance from the Earth to the Sun is about one hundred and forty-nine million, six hundred thousand kilometres. Decimal places are useless here. Instead we count significant figures: the digits that carry meaning, starting from the first one that is not zero.

To two significant figures, the distance is one hundred and fifty million kilometres. The first two significant digits are one and four; the next digit, nine, rounds the four up to five. The zeros that follow are placeholders, keeping the number the right size.
For small numbers, the leading zeros do not count. Zero point zero zero four seven three, to two significant figures, is zero point zero zero four seven. The first significant figure is the four.
?? Round sixty-two thousand eight hundred to one significant figure.
=> The first significant figure is six; the next digit is two, so round down. Sixty thousand.
## Sensible accuracy

Here is the wisdom behind rounding. An answer should not pretend to be more precise than the information it came from. If you measure a room with a tape as about four point two metres by three point eight metres, and multiply to get the area, a calculating machine says fifteen point nine six square metres. But your measurements were only good to a tenth of a metre, so an honest answer is about sixteen square metres.

I once watched a junior clerk at a railway company report that the average passenger travelled twelve point three eight four six two miles. The manager asked him whether he had measured each passenger's journey to the nearest yard. He had not. The figure became twelve miles, and the clerk became wiser.
?? A recipe says to share a cake costing seven pounds among three people. A machine says two point three three three three pounds each. What is a sensible amount?
=> Two pounds thirty-three pence each, which is two decimal places, the precision of our money. One penny will be left over, which Mrs Blewitt would give to the cat.
## Rounding and estimation together

Rounding to one significant figure is the quickest way to estimate. Three hundred and eighty-seven times four point one: round to four hundred times four, about sixteen hundred. The exact answer is one thousand five hundred and eighty-six point seven. A fine estimate.
## Summary

To round, look at the next digit: five or more rounds up, four or less rounds down. Decimal places count digits after the point. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, with zeros as placeholders. And answers should be no more precise than the measurements behind them. Next time, powers and roots, the beginnings of a very grand idea. Until then, my dear friend, good night, to the nearest night.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we face one of the great puzzles of the schoolroom, a rule that generations of children have chanted without understanding: minus times minus makes plus. The poet W. H. Auden, born some years after my time, wrote a little rhyme about it: "Minus times minus is plus, the reason for this we need not discuss." Well, we shall discuss it.
Our road map: positive times negative; negative times negative; three ways to see why; and a story about Augustus De Morgan.
## Positive times negative
Start gently. Three times minus two means three lots of minus two. Three debts of two pounds each.

In plain words: three debts of two pounds is a debt of six pounds. Minus six. And since the order of multiplying does not matter, minus two times three is also minus six. A positive times a negative is negative.
## Negative times negative
Now the puzzling one.
Minus three times minus two is plus six. Here are three ways to see why. Choose whichever you like best, and ignore the others with my blessing.
## First way: the pattern

Watch what happens as we multiply minus two by smaller and smaller numbers. Three times minus two is minus six. Two times minus two is minus four. One times minus two is minus two. Zero times minus two is zero. Each step, the answer goes up by two.

Now carry on the pattern. Minus one times minus two should be two more than zero: plus two. Minus two times minus two: plus four. Minus three times minus two: plus six. The pattern insists. If minus times minus were anything other than plus, the pattern would break, and mathematics does not like broken patterns.
?? While I pour. Continue the pattern: what is minus four times minus two?
=> Plus eight. Each step the answer goes up by two: six, then eight.
## Second way: turning around

Think of multiplying by minus one as turning around on the number line, facing the opposite direction. Multiply once by minus one, and you face left. Multiply twice, and you have turned around twice, so you face right again. Reversing a reversal faces you forwards.
Our language works the same way. "I am not unhappy" means I am, more or less, happy. Two negatives cancel. Though I grant you that "not unhappy" is a very English way of saying it.
## Third way: debts and time

Suppose you are losing two pounds a day, to a gambling habit perhaps, though I trust not. That is a change of minus two pounds per day. Now, three days ago, were you richer or poorer than today? Richer, by six pounds. Minus three days, times minus two pounds a day, gives plus six pounds. Going back in time, a loss becomes a gain.
?? Try one. Minus five times minus four.
=> Two negatives, so the answer is positive. Five fours are twenty. Plus twenty.
## The rules in short
Same signs give a positive. Different signs give a negative. That is the whole rule.
Plus times plus is plus. Minus times minus is plus. Plus times minus is minus.
And the same rule works for division, because division undoes multiplication. Minus twelve divided by minus three is plus four. Minus twelve divided by three is minus four.
?? What is minus eighteen divided by minus six?
=> Same signs, so positive. Eighteen divided by six is three. Plus three.
## De Morgan's puzzled father

Now a story about a real Victorian. Augustus De Morgan was born in 1806 in India, at Madurai, where his father served with the East India Company. He became the first Professor of Mathematics at the new University of London, later called University College, in 1828, when he was only twenty-one or twenty-two. He was a brilliant teacher and a famously witty writer.

In 1831 De Morgan wrote a book called On the Study and Difficulties of Mathematics, and in it he set a puzzle. A father is fifty-six years old and his son is twenty-nine. When will the father be twice as old as the son? If you work it through with algebra, the answer comes out as minus two. De Morgan concluded that the question was absurd: the father will never be twice as old in the future. Notice, though, what the minus two is quietly telling us. Two years ago, the father was fifty-four and the son was twenty-seven, and fifty-four is exactly twice twenty-seven. The negative number was simply pointing into the past.

So even the great De Morgan, in 1831, was uneasy about what a negative answer meant. If you feel uneasy too, you are in very distinguished company. Mathematics took centuries to make peace with negative numbers, and nobody expects you to manage it in one evening.

De Morgan also enjoyed a riddle about his own age. He said that he was x years old in the year x squared. He was forty-three in 1849, and forty-three squared is 1849. I have always envied him; I shall never manage it myself.
## Summary

A positive times a negative is negative. A negative times a negative is positive: you can see it from the pattern, from turning around twice, or from going back in time. Same signs make plus, different signs make minus, for multiplying and dividing alike. Next, we turn to factors, multiples and primes, the building blocks of numbers. Until then, my dear friend, may all your negatives come in pairs.

Good day, my dear friend. You have chosen the refresher, which tells me you have places to be and a mountain to climb. Splendid. This lecture gathers up the whole of base camp's first stretch, whole numbers and the four operations, in one brisk walk. If anything feels rusty, the full lectures are there in the catalogue, and Euclid will keep your seat warm.
Our road map: place value; adding and subtracting; multiplying; dividing; and negative numbers.
## Place value
We write every number with ten digits, and a digit's worth depends on its place. In three hundred and forty-seven, the 3 means three hundreds, the 4 means four tens, the 7 means seven ones.

Each place is worth ten times the one to its right. So multiplying by ten moves every digit one place left, and dividing by ten moves them one place right. Zero holds empty places open: two hundred and five has no tens, and the zero says so.
?? Quickly: what is forty-seven times ten, and what is that divided by a hundred?
=> Four hundred and seventy. Divided by a hundred, four point seven. Each digit moves two places right, past the decimal point. We shall meet decimals properly very soon.
## Adding and subtracting
The pairs that make ten are one and nine, two and eight, three and seven, four and six, five and five. To add in your head, make a ten. Eight and five: eight and two make ten, three left, thirteen.
For bigger numbers, add by places, big parts first.
To subtract, take away a round number and adjust, or count up as shopkeepers do. Sixty-two take twenty-seven: sixty-two take thirty is thirty-two, then add back three. Thirty-five.
Remember that the order does not matter for adding, but it matters very much for subtracting.
?? Ninety-one take away forty-six, any way you like.
=> Forty-five. For instance, forty-six up to fifty is four, fifty up to ninety-one is forty-one, total forty-five.
## Multiplying

Multiplication is repeated adding, and order does not matter, so four sevens equal seven fours. The friendly tables: double for twos, double twice for fours, half of ten lots for fives, ten lots minus one lot for nines.
For bigger numbers, split into places, and let every part meet every part.
That grid of meetings, twenty with ten, four with ten, twenty with three, four with three, will reappear in algebra when we expand brackets. Keep it in your pocket.
?? Nineteen times six, by rounding.
=> Twenty sixes is a hundred and twenty. Take away one six. A hundred and fourteen.
## Dividing
Division is fair sharing, and it undoes multiplication. Fifty-six divided by eight? Ask: eight times what is fifty-six? Seven. For bigger numbers, split cleverly.

Remainders need common sense: thirty people in compartments of eight need four compartments, not three and three quarters. And one firm rule: you can never divide by zero, because no number times zero gives anything but zero.
?? A hundred and twelve divided by eight, by halving three times.
=> Fifty-six, twenty-eight, fourteen. The answer is fourteen.
## Negative numbers

Picture the number line, a road with zero in the middle, positive numbers to the right and negative numbers to the left. Adding walks right, subtracting walks left, and you may walk straight past zero.
Taking away a negative is the same as adding: cancelling a debt makes you richer.
And for multiplying and dividing: same signs give plus, different signs give minus.
Turning around twice faces you forwards again. Augustus De Morgan, in his book of 1831, puzzled over a negative answer to a question about a father's age. You may puzzle too, in excellent company.
?? Minus twenty-four divided by six.
=> Different signs, so negative. Minus four.
## Summary

Place value, making tens, splitting into parts, division as undoing, and the sign rules. That is base camp's first stretch. Next, we look at the building blocks of numbers: factors, multiples and primes. Onward, my dear friend. The mountain will not climb itself, though I have known Euclid to try.

Good day, my dear friend. Here is the second refresher, for the busy climber. In one lecture we shall walk through factors, fractions, decimals, percentages and ratio. If anything trips you up, the full lectures are waiting in the catalogue, each a little slower and gentler.
## Factors, multiples and primes

A factor divides a number exactly: the factors of twelve are one, two, three, four, six and twelve. A multiple is in the times table: twelve is a multiple of four. A prime has exactly two factors, one and itself: two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen. Every whole number above one is built from primes in exactly one way.
⟦60=2\times 2\times 3\times 5⟧
The highest common factor of twelve and eighteen is six; the lowest common multiple of four and six is twelve.
## Fractions
The denominator, on the bottom, says how many equal parts; the numerator, on top, how many we have. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number for an equivalent fraction.
To add or subtract, make the denominators match first, and never add the bottoms.
?? Three quarters take away two thirds.
=> Twelfths for both: nine twelfths take eight twelfths is one twelfth.
